Name: Sed Chapman
Question: How do you shop for rice?
Answer: I can’t remember the last time I shopped for rice. This doesn’t mean the rice we eat, and we eat rice everyday, is free, it just means that we don’t go to the store. This is what happens when one lives on a rice farm; we just don’t sell all we harvest. We keep the family rice supply in a large cooler in the barn. When we need more rice for the house, I go out to the barn and wrestle one of these 30kg bags into the car and go off to the rice polishing machine. These machines are all over the place in rural areas. I imagine they are less common in big cities. They are a simple operation. You pour your bag of unpolished rice in the bin and it polishes it up and spits it out nice and white. You can get your rice polished to varying degrees depending on how you like it: 50%, 75%, normal, extra white, or super polished. The price for polishing 30kg of rice is 300¥ and takes about 5 minutes. And they even have a broom and dustpan for when you spill. After the polishing is done, I'll wrestle the bag back into the car and take it home. Japanese houses often have rice containers in the kitchen. They come in different sizes. Ours is the 30kg version. Polishing the rice heats it up a bit, so we'll usually let it sit in the open bag for a day before we put it in the rice bin. It's a bit hard to see, but there is a small door, slightly open on the bottom of the rice bin. Above the door there are a couple of levers which, when pushed, will allow one or two portions of rice to be dropped into the small container on the bottom. These portions are then transferred to the pot used in the rice cooker. Many of you will already know this but, when making Japanese style white rice, it is good to wash it before cooking. Put the desired amount in the rice cooker bowl and add water. Work the rice with your hands and keep adding and pouring off the water until the pour off is clear. Then add the necessary water you will need to cook it. Most people will use normal tap water to cook their rice. Try using a purer water (not tap) when cooking your rice and see if you notice a difference. Would you like to hear about how the rice I just brought back home got into the rice cooler in the barn? Yes? read on. You might want to pack a lunch. Starting in early spring the fields are harrowed in preparation. The soil is turned over and all is made ready to receive the rice seedlings. The rice seedlings start as seed. Most people get their rice seed from the local agricultural cooperative. Actually, most people get their rice seed from JA. JA is the humongous Japanese agricultural association. JA is really BIG ag! The seedlings come in mesh bags and are placed on vats of water with certain chemicals to spur the seed to sprout. After the seeds start to sprout they are put into the seedling trays. These trays are made of plastic and are about 45 cm long and 30 cm wide. They are put on a conveyor belt and dirt is added. Continuing along the conveyor the dirt gets a light spray of some concoction that works to prevent rice type diseases. Next the newly sprouted rice seed is added, then another layer dirt. The trays are then put into temporary heating rooms for a week or ten days. Once the seeds have sprouted enough that they are poking up out of the dirt, the trays are transferred to greenhouses. They rice sprouts will stay in the greenhouse for another few weeks. They are watered from time to time and the temperatures of the house is adjusted. Once they have gotten to the desired height, it is time to plant. The trays with the seedlings are loaded on to racks on the back of trucks and taken to the field. These small white trucks, known a kei tora (kei trucks) are the workhorses of Japanese agricultural concerns. They are small, sturdy, four wheel drive trucks. A very common sight in rural Japan. Their city brothers are the kei vans one sees everywhere in the bigger cities. The seedlings are taken to the fields and are transferred to the rice planting machine. Grabbing one side of the tray of rice, you lift up and insert a flat plastic tray This insert, with seedlings on top, is carried to the rice planter and either put into the chutes leading to the planting device or put in racks for replenishing the chutes as needed. The planting device grabs a small clump of seedlings and plants it just so, according to the presets. If you look at the photo below you will see some box like things behind the driver. These boxes contain fertilizer that added as the seedlings are added. Up and down the field goes the planting machine. Back and forth to the greenhouses go the little trucks. The Japanese have this all figured out to a nicety. The field is of such and such a size, therefore they will need X number of trays of seedlings to plant. These days almost no one plants by hand. Sometimes you see school kids planting by hand. There are also tourist spots where gals in colorful clothing and straw hats will plant by hand for the cameras. Between planting in the spring and harvest in the fall there are various measures taken to combat weeds, insects, and rice diseases. Some people have started to use remote control helicopters for this. Come fall, the rice has turned yellow-golden in color and the stalks are bent over under their own weight. Harvest time again sees the kei trucks come into action this time there are grain hoppers on the back. The combine enters the field and cuts the rice stalks, that are waist high, off a few inches above the ground. Then, through a ridiculously complicated set of gears, rollers, belts and pulleys, it draws the rice stalks into the machine and separates the stalk from the grain. The stalks are cut up and spit out the back of the machine and the grain is deposited in a holding tank inside the combine. When the holding tank gets full a buzzer sounds and the driver goes over to the waiting kei truck and empties the rice into the grain hopper on the back of the truck. Most, but not all, of the cutting of the rice is done by combines. Some fields are inaccessible by combines and some oddly shaped fields have places where the combine can't operate well and then there are the places that it's just easier for all to just do it by hand. In these cases, out comes the sickle and it's stoop and cut time. The sheaves of rice are then fed into the combine. When the grain hopper is full it is time to take the rice to the rice dryer. The rice that comes out of the field has too high a water content and needs to be dried out a bit before the next stage. After the rice is sufficiently dried it is transferred from the dryer to overhead hoppers. Pipes lead down from these hoppers to the husker and separator machine. This machine separates the rough outer husk from the grain. This is done by feeding the grains through rollers that crack the husk without damaging the grain. The grains are then fed into the scale that holds the rice bag. The husks are blown outside to collect in giant piles. These piles of rice husks are sometimes used for ground cover, but are usually just spread out on the field and plowed under or burned then plowed under. The rice that is fed into the scale machine goes through one last sifting to clean out any remaining fluff. The standard bag of unpolished rice is 30kg (66lbs). Before the bag is put on the scale a metal contraption is put in the bag to keep the bag upright as it fills with rice. Somewhere around 29kg a beeper goes off alerting you to the fact that it's almost ready for a new bag. The flow is automatically stopped at 30kg and the now full bag is taken off the scale and a new empty bag added. Then you hit the lever and the new bag starts to fill. And so it goes. The full bags have to be tied off and stacked. I always stack in layers of five. Each layer laying crossways over the ones below. This is a sturdy way to stack bags of grain. Now 30kg may not sound like a lot of weight, but they are not all that easy to get a good grip on, not to mention the fact that you are lifting 30kg from the scale, then trying it off, then it putting in the stacks - all this adds up to some back discomfort the following morning. Around 60 bags an hour is about average. Once all the rice has been bagged, it is time to call the rice buyer, usually JA, to come pick it up. A couple of guys in a flatbed truck show up and take all your surplus to the rice station. Each bag is checked for quantity and quality and is given a grade. Higher grades earn more money. The bags are then all emptied into a giant grain silo and sold to rice dealers. The rice dealers then package it and sell it to the stores. Somewhere along the line the rice has to be polished. What many consumers are unaware of is that the 'best' rice comes from a particular set of fields on a particular farm. What you get in the store is more of a blended average. When I ask Japanese farmers where is the best rice? They usually respond with, rice that is grown in the hills. They say the water is better the higher you go. Apparently there is a limit. True mountain rice is not as good as the stuff grown in the foothills. My advice to anyone who will listen, is to use as pure a water as you can get when cooking your rice.

Question: Did the Japanese fear the Marines in the beginning of World War 2?
Answer: Many years ago I had conversations with several former Japanese soldiers and sailors. We all worked in the same school and would sometimes, as is common in Japan, go out for food and drinks. At first I was hesitant to ask about their war experiences, but once I became a known entity, both the asking and answering was commonplace. I never asked if they “feared the Marines”, but did ask about what the worst things they experienced. Naturally enough, the worst thing was having friends killed. Being hungry was also often mentioned. Another thing that was mentioned more than once - and this sort of relates to the question - is being shelled by large caliber artillery; specifically being shelled by big naval guns. I remember being told that they much preferred being under fire from small arms. At least they could fight back; but with the big guns of the navy, all they could do was dig a little deeper. I didn’t get the impression that it mattered much if the guys shooting at them were Marines or Army. Interestingly, being attacked by air wasn’t as bad as naval bombardment. I guess it had to do with their being a bit of forewarning. I remember one guy saying (on Saipan) he had a piece of naval shell cut down a good sized tree he was hiding behind. Didn’t touch him.

Question: Are Japanese people sick of having so many foreigners visiting their country? What do they really think?
Answer: First off, your question makes it sound like you think all Japanese - from boondocks Hokkaido to Kyoto to the beaches of Okinawa - to have the same opinions. Japan isn’t some sort of hive; experience and opinions differ depending on circumstances. Where I live - rural Hokuriku - I never see foreign tourists, heck I rarely see Japanese tourists. So, people here don’t have much of an opinion on the current state of tourism. On the other hand, my daughter lives in Kyoto. She lives right down town in Shijo near Karasuma. Now if you’re unfamiliar with Kyoto, this is one of the main tourist spots in the city. The other day I went to visit her. There was no problem driving in and finding a [too expensive] place to park. I was a little early and had to kill some time before she got back from work, so decided to go to a convenience store and get something to snack on. Oh my but the sidewalks were packed with foreigners aimlessly wandering around; making it difficult for anyone with someplace to go and something to do. At the conbini (that’s what they call a convenience store) there was a line out the door! WTF!! Later I said I wanted to go to a nearby restaurant that I liked. Daughter put the nix on the idea saying that we’d never get in became of all the tourists. We ended up using rental bikes and getting away from the tourist blast zone. Daughter says that the tourist influx is something that locals are more or less putting up with. The lack of tourism thing was so bad during the covid period that many businesses were hard pressed. So these crowded times are endured for the sake of others. The problem seems to be that the current tourist boom is relentless. It used to be that there were rises and falls of tourism, but now it’s 24/7/365. I’ve been going to Kyoto on and off for nearly 40 years and these days the experience leaves something to be desired. I wouldn’t go so far as to say people are sick of the foreign tourists as much as they would like it to calm down a bit. On a side note, if the powers that be could somehow ban cellphones, selfies, and tick-tock the Kyoto experience would be far nicer.

Question: What is the one in a million coincidence you have ever had?
Answer: Don't know about how one in a million, but.... It was the winter of 1978 and I was bumming around Europe going to the train stations at night and using my rail pass instead of paying for a hotel room. This made for some strange side trips. Anyway, I had planned on arriving at Heathrow with no money and flying back home to California. But the fates decided differently. There was a bad snow storm and some sort of a strike that shut things down for days. Did I mention that I was flying standby? As a side note the Iranian Revolution had driven out the Shah and the airport was packed with Iranians trying to get home. Stuck in Heathrow with no money and no plane seat in sight. I decided to go into the city and see if I couldn't rustle up some luck. So I'm walking down the street and come across a bakery. Ah! Says I, day old bread might be cheap or even free. I go in the shop and tell the girl behind the counter my story. She looks at me for a long second and says, "I know you, I'm Susan XX, we were in elementary school together." Small world. Improbable is appropriate, I think. Got something to eat and a great memory. Those days and nights in Heathrow still make me laugh at all the weird, happy, lucky things that happened there.

Question: How was it like in the terrible disaster taking place in Ishikawa, Japan? What were you doing and how did you and other people react to the earthquake?
Answer: I was about 40km (25 miles) from the epicenter of the earthquake. I was on the sofa when the big one struck. It went on far longer and stronger than the many other earthquakes I’ve experienced. At first shake, I thought earthquake. After a few seconds I thought, ‘Oh, this is a long one”. After another 10 seconds with increasing intensity I thought, “Oh this is not good”. I decided that the best course of action was to get under the kitchen table. Standing up, the intensity of the shaking was such that I had to take a wide stance and hold on to a chair for balance. More intense shaking. I open the door the room with the table and Dog was standing in the hall looking at me with the question, “Is this supposed to be happening?” I started to feel a bit of motion sickness. I told dog that, things were going to be okay and decided that maybe we would be better outside this old house. Then the shaking gradually stopped. It’s a strange feeling post earthquake when the shaking has stopped. Just a few seconds before things are shaking, dishes are clanging in the sink, stuff is falling off shelves, the whole house is moving back and forth and up and down, then nothing. I knew without being told that the epicenter was somewhere on the Noto Peninsula to the north of me; they got badly hit a few years back and the shaking was similar, but far shorter and less intense. My friend who lives near a Japan Self Defense base said that within minutes of the quake the base went into action and base personnel were pouring back into base, having their New Year’s holiday put on hold. They didn’t have to wait for orders from Tokyo, they knew - everyone knew - this was a bad one. Another friend, a firefighter, was just sitting down to the New Year’s dinner feast when it struck. He didn’t bother to await orders and immediately went to the station. The same for another friend at city hall. He is part of the disaster response team. He too, immediately went to the office to help coordinate with other local authorities. The response was wide ranging and immediate. Helicopters from Komatsu and Shiga were in the air very soon after the quake. The dedication of those involved with disaster response should be commended. It could have been a lot worse, but prior preparation, practice, and experience, on the part of the citizenry and authorities went far to alleviate the inevitable suffering from such an event.

This wasn’t my first earthquake experience, not by a long shot, but it’s been years since I felt that the best thing to do was get under the table. There have been numerous aftershocks, but none like that big one. It looks like things have calmed down; at least for now. Let’s hope big aftershocks don’t come. Question: What if the Shinto gods and goddesses of Japan had maintained their central role in Japanese spirituality, without being overshadowed by Buddhism or other religions?
Answer: There’s really no overshadowing being done. Both belief systems exist and are practiced at the same time. As far as religion goes, you will also find a wide variety of beliefs and levels of devotion. I think it is fairly safe to say that most Japanese are nominally Buddhist and nominally Shinto. I am putting aside the question of whether or not the animistic beliefs of Shinto constitute a religion. *I'm not going to deal with any questions about Yasukuni Shrine or state Shinto or any of that troll bait, so DON'T ASK! Generally speaking, Buddhism gets the afterlife and Shinto gets everything else. The afterlife part is easy to get; they hold the keys. Both in and out. The Shinto part is pretty easy as well. In Christianity there are Saints for this and that, with GOD above all. Shinto has, instead of saints, bunches of gods; gods whose portfolios includes the sea, the mountains, rice fields, birth, getting into a good school, and on and on, and any combination you can think of. There really isn't a GOD above. So, when little kids start going to school mom will attach a Shinto amulet, to their school bag, that is supposed to provide some protection while crossing the street. Kids are well drilled on traffic safety as well. In the room just outside the delivery room in the hospital, the bed is festooned with amulets concerning safe birth. There are doctors in the delivery room. Amulets come in many forms; tiny bags, pieces of paper, wood, etc. If you know what you are looking for they are a common sight. Weddings are also a Shinto shindig. (These days the Shinto rituals are often skipped) Often followed by 'over the top' receptions. The 'legal' marriage is a bureaucratic affair carried on at city hall with no fanfare. This is not to say that Buddhism does not have their share of Buddhist 'saints' that help out in the here and now. It is just that the Shinto gods have a greater market share. Saying that, Buddhist beads worn on the wrist are a common sight. They may be a sign of devotion or a fashion statement or both. As to how important a role religion plays in one's life? I would say that, generally speaking, not as much as one might think. They don't go to 'church' every Sunday. Their observances tend to be tied to the calendar. There are 'feast' days and anniversaries, so to speak. Many houses have a Buddhist altar where one can pray to & for their ancestors. Priests will come on 'special' days to add their bit for a small fee. These family altar tend to be the province of the elder generation. In some houses, a bowl of rice will be placed before the altar as an offering. The previous days offering being carried back to the kitchen for consumption. There is often a Shinto altar, as well. Some people pray at these everyday and some do not. Both altars are often the site of 'special requests'. Just how the intersection of devotion, ritual, and habit is navigated is, as one comes to see, varied. All of this leaves aside the 'new' and 'new-new' religions that are, necessarily, proselytizing and demanding much more adherence. When one is approached on the street, like I was so often in Nara by the Aum Shinrikyo, they are always of the newer brands. I think it would be safe to say that religion in Japan is alive and well, but is far less demonstrative than its Western counterparts. Sort of like the Japanese themselves.

Question: What would you do if you were studying your genealogy and discovered that an ancestor (in 1830s, United States) owned slaves?
Answer: My brother is the keeper of the family tree stuff. It's been handed down for generations and is more than a list of names and dates. There are often short passages about the person. The passages make for interesting reading. There is a sequence from the mid-late 1800's that has always stuck with me. I wish I had the document to check, but alas. The entry about Grandma B had the following: "She never forgave Old Abe for freeing her n—-ers." Interestingly, her daughter "married a noted abolitionist." I'll bet Granny B just loved that. Along this same theme - My father was a SNCC volunteer in Mississippi and Alabama in the 1960’s. He tells a story of staying with a black family out in the boondocks. They asked his last name and when told, they asked if he were related to XX Chapman a former slave holder from long past. Dad said, "Could be." The response from a guy on the porch drinking shine was, "Hell, your people might have owned my grandmother." "Could be." Big laughter ensued. Maybe I should point out that Dad's people came to California before the Gold Rush and the person in question was no relation. And from my mother's side - Mom's father was for a time the WW2 Inspector General of the Western Defense Command. Amongst his duties was to oversee the incarceration of Japanese Americans. Many decades later Mom was living in an old folks home with more than a few who suffered from that ignominy. She told them of her father's position. It made no difference to them. They accepted her for who she was. There was a robust Japanese American community in that home and Mom was always invited to their shindigs. It probably helped that Mom had a granddaughter that could squeak out Japanese children's songs in flawless Japanese. Those ladies would burst into tears hearing the the little girl sing songs from their childhood. If someone is trying to guilt trip you about something you had no hand in, they are mightily in the wrong. That was then, this is now. It is all about becoming.

Question: Have you ever accepted a ride as a hitchhiker?
Answer: How about… It was the winter break of 1975-6 that I hitchhiked from Berkeley to San Antonio, Texas (@ 1700 miles / 2700 km). There were some long and memorable car rides going. The one that particularly stands out was being picked up by a Mexican guy on his way back to his family in Juraez. I went to sleep on the sofa in the living room. When I opened my eyes in the morning, I was greeted by squeals of delight as his two daughters went laughing and running to their mother in the kitchen to report that, yes, the gringo on the sofa had blue eyes. But that isn’t the ride I want to share. That ride came on the way back. I was some miles out of San Antonio on the side of the road pretty much in the middle of nowhere holding a cardboard sign with LA written on it in big black letters. The sun was starting to go down and there was a hella cold wind blowing. Who knew that West Texas could be so bitterly cold. I was not looking forward to camping in some West Texas gulch. Anyhoo, some dude in beat up VW beetle, with mismatched fenders and an 8-track, pulls over. I get in and off we go. He gives me the usual spiel about having to meet a friend further up the road. I had heard this often. I knew he was giving himself an easy out if we didn’t get along. I wasn’t worried. This beat up VW Bug, like many of its kind, had a weak heating system. In the case of this Bug, the amazing amount of icy cold wind that was blasting in from the various crevices on the dash and the front part of the underside, not to mention the broken latch on the wing window, so overpowered the weak heater, that he was constantly having to blow on his fingers to keep them warm. After a bit of chit chat, I told dude that I had some duct tape and that maybe I could do something about some of the drafts. He told me to go for it. Breaking out the duct tape I proceeded to feel for and tape over the icy winds entering the car. After a bit of work the inside started to heat up a bit, or, at least, got bearable. Dude asks if I would like to have a bowl? “Sure,” say I. He says the makings are under the seat. I reach under the seat and pull out a moonlighter with some buds, shake, a pipe, and a match book. I clean a bit; separating stems, seeds, and VW seat hair, fill the pipe, get it started and hand it to dude. (Do you youngins even know what I’m talking about?) He takes a satisfied puff or two and hands it to me. Oh man, rank seeds apoppin dirt weed. Stuff was nasty. Though it was well before the green revolution, I happened to be in possession of some fine green goodness from northern California. I resisted the urge to roll down the window and empty the pipe into the West Texas darkness, but did ask dude if he would like to try some of what I had. He said he would. After a toke or two and enjoying the the increased warmth of the car, he turned to me and said, “Man, you ain’t getting out till we get to California.” And so we headed west through the night.

Question: What was Japanese life like during the American occupation?
Answer: Location, location, location is the only correct and logical answer. The other answers mostly allude to the appalling conditions in metropolitan areas, as if all of Japan consisted of Tokyo, Osaka, and other large industrial areas. Then as now, Japan is more than Tokyo, Kyoto, and Hiroshima. Reading the answers to this question, and many other questions concerning Japan, one can too easily get the impression that Japan consists of solely of Tokyo and Kyoto; that going so far as to visit Sapporo, Kanazawa, or Fukuoka constitutes traveling the “unbeaten tracks in Japan”. That may have been true for Isabella Bird, but hardly holds true for current times. I can see that this digression has leaned a bit too much toward rant. I apologize and will return to the question of life during the occupation. Over the years I have had many conversations with people who lived through the occupation. Their stories and experiences vary widely depending upon location. The experiences of those in the big cities and areas that were bombed are generally pretty bleak; a hard scramble for existence. With food, shelter, and medicine being of primary concern. I will leave those stories to the other answers and the easily google-able. (The surprising number of Chat GTP answers is disheartening) Life in rural Japan was vastly different. Again, it must be pointed out that rural Japan comes in many degrees. For our purposes, I will be referring to the Nth degree of rural Japan: places that did not have airports, railheads, large ports, or even what might be termed a city center. In fact, calling these places a “city” would be a misnomer. This mostly holds true for today, as well. Just because it says such-and-so city on the map doesn’t mean that it resembles in any way Tokyo, or even Okayama. The rural Japan of the Nth degree was, and is, not accessible by plane, train, or in many cases bus. There are great swaths of Japan that are like this. Nary a tourist; neither foreign nor domestic trod these unbeaten tracks. Nth degree rural Japan must be distinguished from the more common rural Japan. Rural Japan, also known as inaka (田舎; いなか) is a rather vague term that refers to just about anywhere outside of the major metropolitan areas. The Nth degree of inaka is douinaka (同田舎; どういなか). The difference between douinaka and, let’s say Shinjuku is staggering. They are hardly on the same planet, let alone the same country. This is, of course, true in many countries. For douinaka Japan the post war upheaval and occupation was far, far less noticeable. By far the greatest change came in the form of the land reform acts of 1946. Under Japan's 1946 land reform, landlords who owned more than the permitted amount had to sell the excess land to the government at a fixed price. The government then sold it at the same price, giving first preference to any tenant who had been farming the land. This was a great boon to the farmers of douinaka. Their land holdings were increased at a time when the prices they could command for food stuffs rose considerably. The land reform benefits were not fully realized until 1947 and beyond, but in the interurm any food surplus commanded very favorable prices. Those city people who had relatives in the douinaka were very lucky indeed. My wife’s father said that these were boom times after the strict controls of war time Japan. I asked about black marketing of rice and vegetables and he was rather vague in answering. I get the impression that such activities were not uncommon. I remember talking to a fisherman from Himi (Toyama) who told me that when they came in with their catch, they would nearly have riots between civilians, fish sellers, black marketers and the auction house representatives. Asking granddad if he ever received food from the occupation authorities, the answer was in the negative. In fact, he said he never even saw an American soldier during that time. The occupation soldiers and staff may have come to the village area, but unless you were at the municipal offices it was unlikely that one would have seen them. I can see that this answer is getting so long as to fall into the TLDR category, so I will end with the salient point that location was critical to the inhabitants of Japan.

Question: Does fat shaming in many East Asian cultures actually help reduce obesity in East Asia or are they typically thinner despite the fat shaming?
Answer: I don’t know about other East Asian countries, but in Japan people don’t usually do “fat shaming”. I suppose kids might tease, but even then it’s not so common. On the other hand, it is not uncommon for Japanese to remark, to the person in question, that they are fat. They will just come right out and say: “You’re fat”. They only do so when the fatness is obvious. That is, when someone’s fatness is beyond chubby. Their saying so is not “fat shaming” it is a statement of fact. It like saying, “The sky is blue” or some other non controversial statement. Calling it “fat shaming” seems to be something that is popular in countries where the overweight population is high. Everyone who visits - that country that shall not be named. FREEDOM!! - is astonished at how many people are grossly overweight. Wikipedia says that the average person in FREEDOM!! weighs nearly 90kg (200lbs) for men and 77kg for women (170lbs). By pretty much any measure that’s a lot. My daughter is a nutritionist at a big hospital in Kyoto. She comes right out and tells her patients, “You’re fat. You have to do something about that.” Her advice to her patients is to eat the traditional Japanese diet in a traditional way. Not ramen, not wagyu beef, not fried chicken. She mimics the Michael Pollan advice to "Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants." She will also tell her charges to walk and exercise more. Typically, traditional East Asian food habits are similar to Michael Pollan’s advice. It is when people stray away that problems occur. There is also the fact that with fewer fat people to compare yourself to, one’s perception of what constitutes overweight is affected.

Question: Has exorcism ever been popular in Japan?
Answer: Oh my but this question is really getting into the deep Miso of Japanese culture. First, let me say categorically that exorcism is not popular in Japan. It may be popular in anime or manga, but in the real world, no. That said, I will relate my slight experience with Japanese exorcism. It was in 1981 or 82, I was living in a rural part of Japan teaching high school. One of the students did not speak. She had a rather hunted and fearful look as she sat silent in the back of the class. I asked one of the teachers about her not speaking and was told, here I am paraphrasing, “that she stopped speaking when the spirit of a miscarried sibling entered her.” Not exactly the Exorcist of Hollywood lore, but nevertheless pretty weird. As you might expect, I was little convinced as to the cause proffered. I asked if she had seen psychologists or psychiatrists and was told that she had. I do not know if she was taking any medication. I do not know what the doctors said about her problem, but was told that a Shinto priest would perform some sort of exorcism on her. There are Shinto purification ceremonies. The ones I know of are Misogi (禊) and another called, Harae or harai (祓 or 祓い). You may have seen photos of people standing under waterfalls as some guy waves a paper and leaf combination, over them. That is Misogi. I believe that Harae is most often seen in the ritual purification and blessing of a plot of land before building. It may also be what they do at shrines to [re] bless and purify the area. I don’t know if these rather common purification rituals were what the young girl was to go through. So, I guess the short answer is that, yes, some types of exorcism do exist in Japan. That said, it would be a gross over simplification to equate Japanese exorcism with those found in other parts of the world.

Question: I've read Kendokas saying they don't do hard parries with katanas, but why do I see a lot of hard parry in the Kenjutsu sparring video of Weaponism (YouTuber)?

Of course, there are times when hard or strong do apply. Like when some dude using Jo-dan gets you hard on the wrist with the point of their shinai. Ouch! The parry is usually a quick flick with the end of the shinai or a kind of a wrist twist parry with the meat of the shinai. Either way, it isn’t hard, quick and firm would be better descriptors. A hard parry would likely leave an opening for another attack. Kendo is much more about speed, quickness, anticipation, and reaction than about strength and power. The dudes that are really good are lightening fast in their reactions. Any opening given and they are on you in a blink of an eye. Many years ago the college team I practiced with went to Kanazawa University for a visit. Eto Sensei of Kanazawa Dai was all Japan champion twice(?) and second twice(?). Now that dude was hella quick. He could double hit you on the body, left - right, so fast it didn’t really make sense. And his kote, oh my! I mean, Eto Sensei would go kote, men, back off, then give you the double do. FAST! He’d be doing this to the college seniors; guys with years and years of kendo. Amazing. Anyhoo, I think that a hard parry is something unnecessary.

Perhaps more to the point, China had a long history of invasion and, as such, had a playbook for such circumstances. They would fight where they could expect a reasonable chance of victory, they would use guerrilla warfare and underground resistance where they could, but more importantly, they would wait. The Chinese, in their many forms, do not get enough credit for putting up the good fight and tying up millions of Japanese troops that could have been used elsewhere.

Question: Why was there no surrender for the Japanese soldiers in World War II?

Question: How powerful was Emperor Hirohito?
Answer: Japanese emperors were not, with one or two exceptions, powerful like their European counterparts. Japanese emperors had neither the power of the purse, nor power of the sword. That is, the emperors did not control the budget nor the military. The power he did have was that he was the only person to have a patina of legitimacy. This legitimacy was derived from being the nominal head of the Shinto religion; the only native religion of Japan. In short he was divine. This doesn’t mean he was a God or even a god. That terminology was wartime propaganda. Let’s just say that he had a “mandate from heaven” that made him super special. As stated above, this “mandate” did not confer strong powers. But it did make him a key person to have on your side. Having him on your side, or perhaps more to the point, having him not stand in opposition, lent a degree of legitimacy to whatever cause was being forwarded. He was a sovereign without tangible power to rule, but with the power to choose sides. It should be noted that those around the emperors had considerable power and often exercised it. The power of Hirohito, if such it can be called, was in his acquiescence to events. I, for one, do not think he was actively involved in policy decisions, but was told by those who wielded real power that “We are going to do thus and so”. At which time he could have voiced his opposition. Moreover, I believe that had he stood too tall in opposition, his reign might well have suddenly passed on to his son - who was too young to rule thus necessitating caretakers - leaving the military in the same nearly unassailable position. Hirohito’s great crime seems, at least to this writer, as one of moral weakness leading to his acquiescence, in essence endorsing, events. Does this let him avoid responsibility? No, but it does shed light on the understanding of his role in shaping events from the mid 1920’s onward.

Question: What is the importance of orgami in Japan?
Answer: Origami (折り紙; おりがみ)is what is known as a recreational art. Many countries have recreational pastimes that can, with practice and refinement, become increasingly artistic in presentation. Japan has several recreational arts that have, over the centuries, become highly stylized and codified in their making and presentation. The most common examples being Japanese flower arrangement: ikebana (生け花; いけばな), and Japanese tea ceremony. Paper folding as a recreational art is not peculiar to Japan - other countries and cultures have similar practices - but, like so many things, the Japanese have taken it to an Nth degree. The question asks about the importance of origami in Japan. I suppose that if origamiwere to somehow instantly disappear, Japanese society would trundle along as if nothing were amiss. The social and cultural importance of origami is not in its presentation, but is found it’s shared experience. Origami has been around for a few hundred years. Once the domain of the upper classes - paper in Japan was, for generations, a labor intensive process called washi(和紙; わし). There are still places that make washi and you can, if you look around, find places where the tourist can make their own paper in the old style. - industrialization and prosperity made paper a cheap commodity and opened origamito all levels of society. In the days before electronic media, origami was one of the things done with kids to pass the time. Grandma would teach the grandkids how to make figures like they were taught by their grandparents. Origami was also incorporated into school arts and crafts classes. I think it would be safe to say that all Japanese have done origami at one time or another. The fact that ALL Japanese have made origami is one of the many things that serve as a common experience in Japan. When people talk about Japanese culture they often point to tea ceremony, anime, traditional festivals, bonsai and the like, but Japanese culture, like any culture, is a large and varied collection of shared experiences that are passed on and through generations. The Japanese recognize the value of such and actively encourage their dissemination and practice. On a more practical level, let me relate a story about origami. For many years I taught in the local elementary and preschools. Over my tenure I noticed a marked and continued decline in the abilities of elementary school first year students to have a solid grasp of many basic skills - reading, writing, manipulation - that kids has previously brought to elementary school. I’m sure there are many educators around the world that have noticed the same. The whys and hows of this phenomenon are a subject for another discussion, but I’m looking sideways at screens. Anyway, I asked a number of elementary school first grade teachers what skills they would like their incoming kids to have. Question: If the Japanese had smashed the American Carrier Fleet at midway, was there a chance the US would have signed a negotiated peace with Japan?

I do not think that the US would have sought a negotiated settlement, at least not in 1942. That said, and here we go with a series of “ifs” that might have led to some sort of negotiated settlement… If the Germans had been [more] successful in their North African campaign and (or?) in their eastern Russian campaigns, I believe the US would have put the war in the Pacific on a temporary hold and put greater efforts into hindering the German attempts to gain a ready supply of oil. Looking at 1942 in hindsight it is easy to say that the US would not have negotiated a settlement, but in 1942 the war was far, far from decided. For much of 1942 it looked like Germany was on a roll and that Russia might actually be the ones going for a negotiated settlement. If that, or Allied defeats allowed Germany to gain ready access to oil, well, then the US must make some devilish choices. My opinion is that they would have gone more heavily into their European First stance and curtailed operations in the Pacific. This would allow the Japanese to consolidate their gains, making subsequent Allied offensives in the Pacific more costly. If the Allies were then to roll back German advances, it is quite possible that war weariness and bloody fighting for unknown places in the western Pacific would have put increased pressure on the US government to find a negotiated settlement. Luckily that is not how things played out.

Question: When Japanese people play the game of rock, paper, scissors, what do they say and how do they play it?
Answer: In Japan, the age old game of Rock, Paper, Scissors is called Janken (じゃんけん), it is played by all ages, but is a particular favorite of the under 12s. The rules are the same (I think) as elsewhere. In Japan the key words are: •Rock: Guu (ぐう). •Scissors: Choki (ちょき). •Paper: Paa (ぱあ). •Begin with rock: Saisho wa guu (最初はぐう) •That's a tie and..! : Aiko desho! (相子) The game starts with one or more of the contestants saying in unison, “Saisho wa guu” (最初はぐう) or “Begin with rock.” When guu is spoken, the players throw down (hold out) rock. Immediately following this the players will say, “janken pon!” and throw down their rock, paper, or scissors on the beat of "pon." Should there be a tie, the players will immediately say, "Aiko desho!”(相子), meaning it's a tie, but they don't stop. On the beat of saying 'sho' of desho, they will throw down again. The process is continued until someone wins. The "Saisho wa guu” or “Begin with rock," is usually only used at the start, but is also used to restart if things get too messy. The entire population has played this game countless times. It is another in a long list of commonalities that the Japanese have. Teachers use it daily. In fact, just the other day I saw a teacher using janken to resolve the serious question of who got the leftover piece of dessert at lunch. Japanese are also adept at doing janken groups. My daughter will sometimes come at me or mom with, “Saisho wa guu," and look expectantly. She does this when she doesn't want to do something, but doesn't want to ask the favor outright. Pro tip: when there is a tie, most people's next throw will be the one that would have won. That is, if the tie involves two papers, the odds are that the other person's next throw will be scissors. I believe this game originated in China and like so many other things Chinese was adopted in Japan. In my family we grew up calling it, "roshambo," but the phrase always met with blank stares. My dad was the one who taught it to us. He may have heard the phrase in San Francisco's Chinatown before the war. So, let’s play, shall we? Saisho wa guu! Janken pon! • • • • • • • • • • • • • Did you win?

Question: Where do raccoon dogs live in Japan?

They are more raccoon like than dog like, but without the “attitude” that many raccoons seem to display. Tanuki generally live in forested areas, but will also inhabit farmland that provides enough cover for them to feel safe. You are unlikely to see them in Tokyo except in their statue form. Big balls and bottles of booze. Looks like he’s going to party. The tanuki, along with the fox, have a folkloric shape shifting reputation. The tanuki statues are often seen around older drinking establishments. The connection seems obvious. Anyhoo, tanuki have achieved a degree of popularity amongst anime fans for their occasional appearances in those mediums. Their appearances in anime and the gaming world far, far exceed their appearances in real life. I’ve spent a fair number of years in rural Japan and have walked many a trail in the outbacks of Japan and have only seen tanuki a handful of times. These days with the declining populations in rural areas, the tanuki has increased its habitat to include abandoned properties within some communities. These abandoned properties offer ‘safe’ islands for tanuki, civits, foxes, and other assorted critters. Lastly, like most wild animals, they make for poor pets.

Question: What is the difference between -chan,-San,-sama,-sa and -kun in Japanese?
Answer: The Japanese are great users of honorifics and titles in everyday speech. Most of you are aware that Japanese regularly attach san(さん) to someone’s name. Going up register, sama or dono is often written, but less often spoken. And going down register the diminutives, chan (ちゃん) and kun (くん) are common. Unless you know what you are doing, it is probably best to stick with sanwhen in regular conversation. Using sama(様) or the diminutives are less likely to achieve the desired effect. Chan (ちゃん) and kun (くん) are common diminutives for girls (chan) and boys (kun). That said, it is not uncommon for chan to be attached to a boy's name. There are other uses of kun, as well. It should be noted that chan and kun are not gender specific in the way Mr and Ms [Miss, Mrs] are.
